   S’pore studying US chip export curbs, seeking ‘trusted access’ for legitimate firms: Josephine Teo

 Ng Wei Kai
 Published   Nov 17, 2026, 04:29 PM
 Updated   Nov 17, 2026, 08:21 PM
 Set as preferred source Listen 中文 SINGAPORE – Singapore is studying new US export rules on artificial intelligence chips and will work to ensure legitimate businesses continue to have “trusted access” to critical AI infrastructure, said Minister for Digital Development and Information Josephine Teo. 
 The authorities are continuing to engage with the US on the scope of the implementation of the rules, as well as with businesses on how the rules will impact operations, she said on Nov 17.
 Her comments came at a panel discussion and in a media interview at an event by American media company Semafor, and follow the new US export rule by the US Commerce Department on Nov 16.
 The new provision governs the export of advanced chips used in training top-end AI models to overseas data centres and will require companies in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil to apply for US licences to import these chips.
 It is meant to clamp down on China’s use of these chips through shipments re-routed via third countries or through remote access to data centres equipped with such chips based in other jurisdictions.
 The issue has come to the fore in recent weeks amid attention on Nvidia, one of the world’s top producers of these chips and its relationship with Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based firm accused of buying Nvidia AI chips and re-routing them to China. 
 There is still a strong basis for continued cooperation between Singapore and Washington on a “whole range of areas”, Teo said, in response to a question about the state of bilateral ties and whether the Megaspeed issue had affected relations. 
 Megaspeed’s alleged role in circumventing US export controls came into focus on Nov 8 after news broke of an affair between its former top executive Alice Huang and former Nvidia chief Jensen Huang.  
 Alice Huang is also suspected by the US of being a Chinese intelligence asset.  
 She and Megaspeed have been the subject of parallel investigations by both the Singapore and American authorities for suspected violations of various laws in both jurisdictions. 
 Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs has said that despite repeated requests, the US Department of Justice and Federal Bureau of Investigation did little to assist its investigations – especially in another case involving Super Micro, a US-based server supplier that has an office in the city-state. 
 Megaspeed is involved in a larger Singapore probe into potential false declarations over the purchase of servers, and is also under scrutiny in the US. 
 It is useful to look at the whole relationship between Singapore and the US in context and “not just one part of it, at one point in time”, Teo said. 
 Cooperation spans many areas, she added, noting that she had recently met US Deputy Secretary of State Chris topher Landau as well as a legislator and another US Cabinet member. 
 Teo added that she was encouraged that leading AI firms such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Google DeepMind, which use these chips to train top-end AI models, have continued to set up activities in Singapore. 
 “We will work with them to expand their footprint and to help them to succeed,” she said.
 It is important that these companies feel confident that AI can be implemented in a trusted way – not just at the enterprise level, but also in terms of how the technology is going to be used on a sustained basis, she added.

 AI at home
 Domestically, however, turning that corporate presence into workplace efficiency remains a work in progress.
 Teo acknowledged a gap between the productivity Singaporeans feel from their personal use of generative AI and how the technology is being used at work.
 AI companies “setting up shop” in Singapore can help plug this gap, she said, citing numbers from Anthropic, which runs Claude, and OpenAI, which is behind ChatGPT.
 The figures show that the city-state ranks highly globally in AI use per capita.
 Anthropic opened a Singapore office and signed a memorandum of understanding with the Government to hold technical exchanges with Singapore’s AI safety, security, and assurance institutions in October, while OpenAI started an applied AI lab here in May. 
 Beyond individual corporate initiatives is a need for shared responsibility in dealing with AI risks, Teo said, referencing how risks are dealt with collectively in aviation. 
 In aviation, manufacturers and airlines work to ensure safety, along with international bodies that set standards. 
 A similar ecosystem will have to be built for AI. While nobody knows what it will eventually look like, it must start somewhere, Teo said. 
 “We can get a coalition of the willing to move on something, we should try and take it as far as possible,” she said, citing a recent call between Singapore, Norway and Finland proposing practical ways forward on issues like reporting of safety incidents.
 Asked about the potential for public pushback against AI adoption that has been seen in other countries like the US, Teo said the Government has to explain the risks of AI when it understands them and say so when it does not. 
 “I think we have to be perfectly honest with our citizens: what we understand and what we don’t understand.”
 Doing so helps to build trust, she said, adding that citizens will also be able to focus on the technology’s benefits and potential harms.
